#3195. Report: Apple job listings detail plans for autonomous AI agents

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the company’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its plans to develop autonomous AI agents:

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Today’s report on the new job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the company could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how quickly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally launched its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

#3194. These Are the Best Early Black Friday Deals on Kindles and E-Readers

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

Because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a new model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

If you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is currently $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The new Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

If you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

If you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, currently marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.)

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

For about $30 more than the X4 Classic, you can upgrade to the Xteink X4 Pro, which happens to be Lifehacker's e-reader Gift of the Year pick. It offers all the perks of the other Xteink devices, with two critical quality-of-life upgrades: A touchscreen for easier navigation, and a temperature-adjustable front light so you can read it in a dark room. (Less obviously, it also has a slightly faster processor that makes the whole thing feel a little snappier.) Right now, the X4 Pro is at its lowest price ever when ordered directly from Xteink: $84, or around 15% off the usual $99 price.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3193. The 'debasement trade' returns after Bessent bond maneuver. Crypto and gold are back in style

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

The conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

Gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

Bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department said last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the plans.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "big toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

"Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold said in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah said. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

"The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah said in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining."

Coltman at 21Shares said the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

Deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh said in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

"The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma."

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, said Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

#3192. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3190. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3189. If You Loved 'The Diplomat,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

The Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

If you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

When a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

It’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating new crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Want more cynical diplomats, secret plans, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and launches a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

This might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

After releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the company is now rolling out the public beta for users looking to try the new features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

The Disney+ and Hulu bundle saves you 52% compared to subscribing individually. For $11.99 per month, you get two services that pair together perfectly. Note: This bundle deal is available even outside of Black Friday, so it's not strictly a seasonal sale, but it's still an excellent saving on a great bundle. If you want even more streaming options, you can add HBO Max for $21.99/month or ESPN for $35.99/month. But the regular Disney+/Hulu bundle is my top pick.

Peacock's Black Friday deals for 2026 have arrived, which is particularly noteworthy as the streaming service didn't offer any last year. The cheapest package is Peacock Select for $2.99 per month (was $8.99), but I recommend the Premium tier, now $8.99, because it includes everything: movies, live sports, originals and more, whereas Select, as the name implies, gives you a pretty limited selection of shows.

Paramount+ has discounted every tier to $2.99 for 2 months ahead of Black Friday. The best package is the Premium tier. You can get full access to the Paramount+ library with ad-free streaming, Showtime originals, and your local CBS station. There's plenty to watch on Paramount, including "Dutton Ranch," "Yellowjackets," every episode of "South Park", NFL (via CBS), and Champions League soccer, and that's just a tiny preview of what's on offer in this library of 40,000+ episodes and movies.

Prime Video add-on subscriptions: deals from $0.99Prime Video add-on subscriptions give you access to additional streaming service libraries within Prime Video. There are big players like Paramount+ and Apple TV, alongside MGM+, Hallmark+, Starz, Crunchyroll, AMC+, BritBox and more. The deals start from $0.99, but my top pick is the AMC+, MGM+ and Starz bundle for $5.49 per month for two months (was $21.99).

Apple TV is 50% off right now, and home to some of the best originals around; Netflix just can't compete when it comes to quality shows you can't watch anywhere else. From "Slow Horses" to "Shrinking" to "Silo," and if you want a comfort watch, try "Trying" or the ever-popular "Ted Lasso." At $6.99 per month for six months, this is one of the best Black Friday deals around, and the perfect chance to enjoy everything Apple TV has to offer.

Here’s your chance to binge on one of TV’s all-time great shows, Mad Men. Up there, IMHO, with other classics, including The Sopranos and Succession, Mad Men will suck you in with its love-em-hate-em characters, plot twists, and period-specific themes. And for just $1.99 a month (for the first two months), you too can experience the dawn and evolution of modern advertising, alongside the charismatic, multifaceted main character, Don Draper (Jon Hamm).

Good morning! It's officially Black Friday week, and there are plenty of great streaming deals to talk about, so it's a good job you've found Tom's Guide Black Friday streaming deals live blog, where we're going to highlights all the very best discounts! There's no time to waste, let's get down to talking about streaming deals...

Prime Video add-on subscriptions are discounted for Black Friday, and if you've not heard of these before, they essentially allow you to access additional streaming services within the Prime Video UI. It's useful if you want all your streaming content to be in (mostly) one place. The discounted options include Apple TV, Paramount+, MGM+, AMC+, Starz, Hallmark+, Lionsgate+, Discovery+, Crunchyroll, and loads more. With deals from $0.99, you will definitely find an add-on subscription for your tastes.

One of the first Black Friday streaming deals for 2026 came from Paramount+, and while others have since appeared, this one remains one of the strongest. Every tier of Paramount+ is discounted down to $2.99 per month for two months, including the top package, Paramount+ Premium. The slogan says it offers a "mountain of entertainment" and I'm inclined to agree. You can read more about the deal in our dedicated article, or if you're already sold, sign up now with the link below.

The Black Friday streaming deal that's caught my attention right now is Crunchyroll. This platform is the place to go for all things anime, and while I'm not an expert, it's a genre I'd love to explore more. I already know I love "Chainsaw Man," so what other anime is out there that I'd love but haven't discovered yet?

The Crunchyroll deals start from $3.99 per month for the basic Fan tier, up to $8.99 (was $17.99) per month for the Ultimate Fan tier, which also includes access to games, manga and the Crunchyroll store. Let's just say I'm tempted by this one.

Apple TV has a strong case to be the most overlooked streaming service. It doesn't offer the overwhelming library size of Netflix, Prime Video or HBO Max, but when it comes to quality original shows, Apple TV is giving the biggest players a run for their money. "Severance," "Slow Horses," "Shrinking" and "Silo" are all great, and the platform also has must-watch originals that don't begin with the letter "s" as well!

Ahead of Black Friday, you can get six months of Apple TV for $6.99 per month, that's a 50% discount, and if you've never had a subscription before, you've got plenty of worthwhile watches to catch up. My first-choice recommendations would be "Trying" (a warm-hearted comedy that's better than "Ted Lasso") and "Black Bird," an excellent and very intense prison drama inspired by true events from 2022.

You won't find many (any?) Black Friday streaming deals cheaper than this one; Frndly TV is $0.99 per month. That's more than 90% off its regular price. Frndly TV isn't the most well-known streamer, but you get access to a large selection of live channels including Hallmark, A&E, History, Lifetime, The Weather Channel and a whole lot more. And there's a whole "On Demand" library, if you've left live TV behind. For less than a dollar per month for three months, it's worth checking out.

YouTube is far the streaming platform I use the most, and while YouTube Premium isn't discounted for Black Friday (unfortunately), YouTube TV is very much on sale. There are two packages to pick from: Sports + News and YouTube TV. We ranked the latter as our top pick of the best live TV streaming service, calling it the best cable TV alternative for most people. So, if you want to check it out for less, YouTube TV is $59 per month for two months (was $82), or the Sports + News package is $49 for six months, which is a massive $132 saving over the course of your discounted sub.

When it comes to Black Friday streaming deals, it's natural to opt for the cheapest tier of a service, and with Peacock that's the Select tier on sale for $2.99 per month. It's a great price, but the Select package...well, it's not so great. It comes with some pretty huge drawbacks. Namely, no movies, live sports, or Peacock originals. And it's ad-supported as well.

Peacock Premium for $8.99 per month (for three months) is the much better balance of price and features. Yes, Premium still has ads (you need the Premium Plus tier for ad-free streaming), but you get movies, live sports (including Premier League soccer), and can watch Peacock Originals like "The Day of the Jackal."

My advice is to pick Premium, even if it costs a little more than Select, because even for a discounted $3 a month, Select has too many limitations for me to recommend.

Disney+ offers some of the best bundles in the business, with its Disney+ and Hulu bundle for $11.99 per month (a 52% saving), the jewel in the crown. To be clear, this isn't actually a Black Friday deal. This discounted rate is available all year, but it's such a great deal that it's proving very popular right now. If you want even more streaming, you can also add HBO Max or ESPN for an additional fee. Nevertheless, the Disney+/Hulu bundle is the spotlight-stealer, because the two services pair together like American cheese on a burger!

There are plenty of worthwhile add-on subscriptions on Prime Video, and many of them are on sale; one of my favorites is MGM+. This platform gives you access to great movies including "Project Hail Mary," "Is God Is," and "Mission: Impossible: The Final Reckoning," but it really shines for bingeable TV; there's "The Institute," which recently dropped its second season, and "From," a compelling dark-thriller show.

You can add MGM+ to your Prime Video account for just $1.99 for the first two months; that's long enough for you to enjoy the best of what the platform offers.

I've already highlighted the great Black Friday deals running on Paramount+ and Apple TV in this live blog. But did you know you can actually score both via Prime Video? Yup, you can add the Apple TV or Paramount+ libraries to your Prime Video account, which saves you having to hop between separate apps on your smart TV or phone. The same deals running directly on the streaming services themselves are also available as a Prime Video add-on subscription, which means Paramount+ for $2.99/month and Apple TV for $6.99/month. So you'll get the same saving, as well.

Want to watch "Michael" with your family over Thanksgiving? Then check out this Starz deal for $2.99/month for two months (was $11.99). Coming via Prime Video, the service is the streaming home of the fan-favorite Michael Jackson biopic, and fans of music movies will also want to check out "Power Ballade" starring Paul Rudd and Nick Jonas. Meanwhile, TV watchers shouldn't overlook "Sweatpea" starring "Fallout'" Ella Purnell. For just $2.99, you're getting plenty to watch now.

I've been waiting for HBO Max to show its hand, and finally it's confirmed its Black Friday deal, and it was worth the wait.

The Basic w/ Ads plan is 50% off, now $5.49/month (was $10.99). That's a great deal for our top-rated streaming service, but what makes this deal such a spotlight-stealer is you get the discounted rate for a full year. Yes, 12 months of HBO Max for 50% off! HBO just one-upped its rivals, which are mostly offering 2 months of savings, with even Apple TV's six months unable to compete. And yes, you can sign up now ahead of the "Harry Potter" show premiering on HBO Max on December 25.

Since it's debut in 2020, I've made it my mission to convince anyone who will listen to stream "Trying" on Apple TV. Coach Lasso gets all the credit, I'm here to tell you this show is the best comfort watch on the platform. It's a wonderfully warm series, now five seasons deep, about a couple (played by Esther Smith and Rafe Spall) trying to adopt. It's funny, with just the right splash of drama, and very much the type of show you could watch on repeat when you need a mood-booster. With Apple TV discounted for Black Friday, I encourage you to give "Trying" a try! I think you'll love it.

One question that always comes up around this time of the year is, "what is Netflix's Black Friday deal?" And I've got bad news on this front, at the time of writing, there is no Netflix Black Friday discount, and I don't expect that to change. Secure in its position as the world's biggest streaming service, Netflix rarely (if ever) offers discounts, and in all my years of Black Friday deal hunting, it's never offered a Black Friday deal. 2026 is looking no different. Of course, stranger things have happened (pun intended!), but I wouldn't bank on Netflix getting a seasonal discount.

Streaming writer Alyse Stanley taking over now! Easily my most anticipated show of the year is "Yellowjackets," a.k.a. "Lord of the Flies" but if you made it girlie pop and gay. I expect this last season to be a glorious trainwreck, since that's been the case with every other season since it's immaculate first run, but that doesn't mean I'm any less excited to see these girls eat each other alive. The fourth and final season just kicked off on Paramount+, and since you can get the streamer for just $2.99 a month right now, I can't recommend this deal enough.

For as long as I can remember, HBO Max has reigned supreme at the top of our best streaming services guide, and the streamer brought back it's epic 50% off deal just in time for Black Friday. Until November 30, you can score HBO Max for just $5.49/month for your first year — down from $10.99/month. That's a steal to watch some of the best shows TV has to offer, like "Lanterns," "The Gilded Age," and "The Pitt." There's plenty of upcoming releases everyone will be talking about to watch in the next year too, like the "Harry Potter" remake in December and new seasons of "A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms," "Heated Rivalry," "The White Lotus," and "The Last of Us" coming later in 2027.

With Amazon hosting deals on streaming devices starting at just $15, there's never been a better time to upgrade your entertainment set-up. These devices bring together all your favorite streaming apps in one place, from Netflix, Prime Video, Disney+ and Apple TV to various free and live TV services. These popular devices tend to sell out quick every year around this time, so my advice is to shop these deals early before supplies run out.

Amaze! Amaze! Amaze! I'm not the biggest sci-fi fan, and even I thought "Project Hail Mary" was an absolute treat. Ryan Gosling is in top form as the charming yet woefully out of his league Ryland Grace, a disgraced scientist now teaching middle school and given the impossible task of saving the world. It's on MGM+, which is just $1.99/month through Prime Video right now.

Full cards on the table: This Disney+/Hulu bundle isn't technically a Black Friday deal, just the regular discounted bundle price, but it's still worth considering if you're looking to save on both services. Granted, we've seen the price drop even further in the lead-up to Black Friday in previous years — for example, last year it was just $4.99/month for the first year. We'll be keeping an eye out for a similar deal and update this guide if it returns, but until then, this bundle is the cheapest way to get both Disney+ and Hulu.

"Frieren: Beyond Journey's End" is an absolute gem for any fantasy fans out there. It follows a near-immortal elf across several human lifetimes as she traces the impact her D&D-style adventuring party had on the world in the years (and sometimes centuries) since they've passed. She's also on the hunt for the most niche spells she can find, which adds a touch of whimsy to the show's heavier themes. Along with "Attack on Titan" and "Blue Lock," it's one of my favorite animes on Crunchyroll, which is marked down to just $3.99 for six months right now for Black Friday.

“Crystal Lake” is the exactly the kind of prequel the “Friday the 13th” franchise deserves. Linda Cardellini is a standout as Pamela Voorhees, while some insane kills, gruesome practical effects and a convincingly re-created ’70s setting make for a bloody good time. You can watch it all on Peacock, which is just $2.99 for their lowest tier right now. Peacock Select is also the cheapest way to stream all your NBC and Bravo favorites.

If your holiday season isn't complete without a Hallmark movie or two, you're in luck. The streamer just added 24 new Christmas movies as part of its annual "Countdown to Christmas," and right now you can get Hallmark+ through Amazon for just $2.25 a month, down from $8.99.

As tempting as all these streaming deals, keep in mind that you won't have forever to snag them. The vast majority of Black Friday streaming deals are only through November 30th, a.k.a. Cyber Monday, with most finishing at midnight on that Monday. So you'll want to get in on the savings while you can! Once these streamers go back to their usual rates, we likely won't see deals this good until this same time next year.

If you love streaming but are a little tight on space — I'm looking at you, my NYC-based pals — then a shiny-new projector may be a more sensible upgrade for your binging pleasure than a traditional TV. And I've got just the projector for you. The Happrun Roku TV Smart Mini Projector is a steal at just $109 from Best Buy, marked down from $299. As the name implies, it features Roku’s easy-to-use user interface. Plus, you get solid 720p HD picture quality with a respectable 150 lumens of max brightness to ensure your movie night is the talk of the block.

#3185. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

The Oura Ring 5 is the world’s smallest smart ring and looks more like a piece of stylish jewelry than a fitness tracker. Though it’s rarely discounted, it’s currently seeing a record-low price of $299 (originally $399) in this early Black Friday deal.

#3183. LiberNovo’s Black Friday sale takes up to 42% off ergonomic chairs

You can spend plenty of time getting your Mac, display, and desk just right. But what about the chair you use every day? Between typing, taking video calls, and leaning back to watch something, your position changes throughout the day. Your chair should be able to keep up.

That’s the idea behind LiberNovo’s ergonomic chairs, which combine support that moves with you and a choice of sizes, including the Maxis range for bigger and taller users. For Black Friday, LiberNovo is taking up to 42% off in the U.S., with chairs starting at $609 and offers running November 19–30.

Adjusting a chair for your desk is one thing. Keeping that support as you change position is another. LiberNovo’s Dynamic Support System links the neck support, backrest, armrests, and seat so they move together as you recline.

The Bionic FlexFit Backrest adds eight flexible panels that contour independently. Rather than relying on a single rigid backrest, the design lets different sections follow your back as you shift or turn. Once you’ve adjusted the chair to fit, the system is designed to maintain contact through those movements with fewer manual readjustments.

Both the Omni and Maxis families offer five recline positions: 105, 115, 125, 135, and 160 degrees. That gives you options for desk work, a more relaxed position for watching a video, and a deeper recline for a break.

A higher weight limit is only part of finding a chair that fits. Taller users also need enough seat depth, a headrest that reaches the right spot, and armrests with room to adjust.

The LiberNovo Maxis range addresses those details with a 52 cm seat depth, a wider backrest with a flared base, and an extended-travel headrest with 140 mm of vertical adjustment and 120 mm of front-to-back adjustment. Its armrests sit lower and offer a wider, longer adjustment range to accommodate larger builds.

LiberNovo recommends Maxis for users approximately 5 feet 10 inches to 6 feet 7 inches tall, with a maximum supported weight of 399 pounds. Maxis is certified to BIFMA X5.11. The seat cushion uses firmer support at the rear and a softer front edge, while a six-spring Controlled Recline System is designed to build resistance progressively as you lean back.

For a shallower seat, the Omni family offers 45 cm and 48 cm configurations. Choosing between the two families starts with fit, then comes down to which features you want.

There are three feature tiers in each family. Omni SE and Maxis Manual offer manually adjusted lumbar support, without a motor or battery. Both retain the flexible backrest, dynamic support, and five recline positions.

The Maxis Electric includes motorized lumbar adjustment and OmniStretch, a five-minute powered stretch sequence used in deep recline.

Omni Pro and Maxis Airflow add Active AirFlow seat ventilation. A fan draws air through the cushion to carry heat away, and an occupancy sensor pauses the fan when you stand up. These models also include a larger 3,000 mAh rechargeable battery.

LiberNovo’s warranty covers the frame and structural components for six years, and electronic components for two years.

U.S. Black Friday prices run from November 19 through November 30. Here’s how the chair-only Basic Bundles compare:

Bundles add another option. The Omni Pro Standard Bundle includes the chair and a footrest for $983. The Maxis Electric Premium Bundle includes the chair, a footrest, and an extra battery for $1,202, down from a listed MSRP of $2,086.

LiberNovo is also offering 30-day price protection on eligible purchases. U.S. gift tiers begin at $800 for a Mouse Pad, $1,000 for an Eco-Comfort three-piece gift set, and $1,200 for an Ergo-to-Go Travel Suite. Qualifying orders of $2,000, $3,000, or $4,000 receive an automatic additional saving of $60, $100, or $180, respectively, without a code.

U.S. shoppers can also choose Klarna Pay in 4 at 0% APR.

Ready to give your desk setup a more comfortable place to sit? Shop LiberNovo’s Black Friday sale to compare Omni and Maxis models, choose your fit, and explore the available bundles through November 30.

Black Friday week is finally here and you know what that means: it's time to save big on your favorite tech. Whether you're looking for a brand new product or wanting to upgrade your existing setup, there's a deal for everyone. If you're on the market for one of the best drones, you've come to the right place.

I review drones for a living (I know, it's a very cool gig) and love flying them in my spare time, too. There's something exhilarating about capturing your world from a bird's eye view. With how far drones have come in the last decade, it's now easier than ever to capture such sights — and you don't need to be an expert, either.

Though more deals are yet to come, I've already found killer discounts on my top-rated quadcopters from DJI, Antigravity and HoverAir. The best deal you can get right now is on the Antigravity A1 Explorer Bundle, which is a whopping $660 off at Amazon. This is a fantastic 360-degree drone that lets you capture every angle possible.

Want something a bit more straightforward? The DJI Flip (with RC 2 controller) is down to its lowest ever price of $449 at Amazon, and it's a phenomenal beginner-friendly and lightweight drone for taking traveling with you. There are more deals to take advantage of, of course, so keep reading for the seven best deals on my favorite drones!

The DJI Flip is a solid mid-range drone, perfect for those looking to upgrade from older DJI models. It captures detailed 48MP stills in all lighting conditions, and records gorgeous 4K/60fps footage. It’s great for content creators as it features many shooting modes, plus it’s built really well and sports a slick design. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller.

The DJI Avata 360's twin lenses let you capture every angle possible, and footage is captured at 8K/60fps, giving you plenty of headroom in post-production. The drone is extremely easy to fly with either goggles or a standard controller, and unlike its primary competition, the Avata 360 does so without breaking the bank. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller, a landing pad, a microSD card, and a backpack.

With omnidirectional obstacle avoidance and forward-facing LiDAR, the DJI Mini 5 Pro is capable of returning home even without GPS. It introduces a few notable upgrades as compared to its predecessor: a 1-inch sensor for improved low-light performance, 225° gimbal rotation, all while retaining a compact form factor. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller, extra batteries, a landing pad, a microSD card, and more.

The DJI Mavic 4 Pro records 6K/60fps video and captures 100MP stills powered by a Hasselblad camera. With a long flight time and 5-star performance across the board, it’s the ideal drone for commercial and personal use. This is the best consumer drone you can buy. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller, a microSD card, a landing pad, and more.

The Antigravity A1 is fitted with tech you’ll find in Insta360's action and 360° cameras, and it lets you capture every angle possible. Footage is shot in 8K/30fps, enabling you to maintain 4K in 16x9 when reframing in post. 55MP stills look great too. Flying the drone is easy (and immersive) with the Vision goggles and Grip controller. The Explorer Bundle includes goggles, controller, extra batteries, and more.

If you want a cheaper option, the Antigravity A1 Follow Me Bundle is a great choice. It comes with propeller guards so the drone can fly safely, and a Watch Remote with touch controls for, well, controlling the A1's settings. One-tap cinematic shots are made easy with this bundle.

Unlike most other drones, you don't need a controller or a smartphone to fly the HoverAir X1, which is why it's a great selfie drone. Simply press the buttons on its body and it will record short-form videos and save them internally. My colleague enjoyed using it a lot and appreciated its surprisingly good obstacle avoidance and subject tracking features such as follow, rocket, and more.
